lesson.title: Basic One-Variable Equations: Undoing What Was Done
lesson.summary: Solving a one-variable equation means isolating the variable by undoing operations in reverse, using inverse operations equally on both sides so the equation stays balanced at every step.
lesson.body:
Picture an equation as a balance scale, with the equals sign as the pivot point. Whatever total weight sits on the left must equal the total weight on the right, and that balance is the entire reason an equation is true. If you add, subtract, multiply, or divide one side of the scale, you must do the exact same thing to the other side, or the scale tips and the statement stops being true. This single idea, keep both sides balanced, is the only rule you truly need to solve any one-variable equation.

Solving means isolating the variable, getting it alone on one side of the equals sign, which requires undoing whatever has been done to it, and undoing operations in the reverse order from how order of operations builds them up. If a variable has been multiplied and then had a number added, you subtract that number first and divide last, peeling operations off from the outside in, the mirror image of how PEMDAS would build the expression from the inside out.

Take 5x minus 7 equals 2x plus 8. There are variable terms on both sides, so the first move is to gather them onto one side using inverse operations: subtract 2x from both sides, which removes it from the right and leaves 3x minus 7 equals 8 on the combined equation. Next, undo the subtraction by adding 7 to both sides: 3x equals 15. Finally, undo the multiplication by dividing both sides by 3: x equals 5. Every move was legal because it was applied to both sides equally, keeping the scale balanced throughout.

Checking the answer is fast and catches almost every careless error: substitute x = 5 back into the original equation. The left side, 5 times 5 minus 7, is 25 minus 7, which is 18. The right side, 2 times 5 plus 8, is 10 plus 8, also 18. Both sides match, confirming x = 5 is correct. Building the habit of checking a solution by substitution, especially on a timed test where a single sign error can slip by unnoticed, is one of the most valuable habits you can carry forward into every equation-solving topic that follows, including the two-variable linear equations in the next chapter.
